title: Working from Home: What the Data Shows
text:
A new survey published by a national research institute suggests that employees who work from home several days a week feel less stressed than their colleagues in offices. The authors of the study, however, point out that the sample included mainly people in well-paid professional jobs. Many respondents also reported that they found it harder to separate work from private life. The report therefore recommends that companies set clear rules about working hours.

Managers have reacted to the findings with caution. Some argue that informal conversations in the office help teams build trust, which is difficult to achieve through screens. Others believe that flexible arrangements will attract talented staff who would otherwise leave the profession. The institute plans to repeat the survey next year with a larger group of workers from manufacturing and retail.

questions.text: According to the survey, how do employees who work from home several days a week feel?
options: They feel less stressed than office colleagues
They work longer hours than office colleagues
They earn more money than office colleagues
They change jobs more often than office colleagues
Remote work should be banned in all companies
The survey was conducted in manufacturing
Informal conversations in the office help teams build trust
Flexible arrangements are too expensive for staff

questions.text: What can be inferred about the sample used in the study?
options: It may not represent workers in every type of job
It included only people who never work from home
It was the largest survey ever conducted
It was designed by the companies themselves

questions.text: Why does the institute plan to repeat the survey with different workers?
options: It has already proven that remote work is better
It wants to test whether the results apply more widely
Managers asked it to remove the findings
The current survey was too short to read

paragraph_translations: Nowe badanie opublikowane przez krajowy instytut badawczy sugeruje, że pracownicy, którzy kilka dni w tygodniu pracują zdalnie, odczuwają mniej stresu niż ich koledzy w biurach. Autorzy badania zwracają jednak uwagę, że próba obejmowała głównie osoby na dobrze płatnych stanowiskach specjalistycznych. Wielu respondentów zgłaszało również, że trudniej im oddzielić pracę od życia prywatnego. Raport dlatego zaleca, aby firmy ustaliły jasne zasady dotyczące godzin pracy.

Menedżerowie zareagowali na wyniki z ostrożnością. Niektórzy twierdzą, że nieformalne rozmowy w biurze pomagają zespołom budować zaufanie, a tego trudno dokonać przez ekrany. Inni uważają, że elastyczne formy zatrudnienia przyciągną utalentowanych pracowników, którzy w przeciwnym razie odeszliby z zawodu. Instytut planuje powtórzyć badanie w przyszłym roku, z większą grupą pracowników z produkcji i handlu detalicznego.
